The present work includes two references to America, and Ben Nicholson was focusing in particular on creating networks in New York at the time that he made this work: a key contact for him at this time was G L K Morris, who was based there. Although distinct from the present work, Rachel Smith has written in her PhD on Ben Nicholson of his focus on the States at this time, which helps to illuminate the context surrounding this work:
'Nicholson and Morrisâs correspondence between the autumn of 1941 and spring of 1942 reveals that both artists particularly valued transatlantic exchange at this time. In September 1941 Nicholson was on a mission to send works to the United States for safe-keeping and potential display. By post he sent Morris a small work, probably his 1941 (painted relief), and Morris responded with gratitude and a statement of nationalised solidarity. He wrote, âIt is a beautiful one, and it does us good to know that England is able to produce things of such quality at the moment.â He explained that, in return, he was sending Nicholson the next number of Partisan Review which included an article explaining âhow I construct picturesâ. Morris also requested more images of recent work by Nicholson and his âcompatriotsâ and responded positively to an ideas posed by Nicholson to highlight the shared interests and mutual support of English and American artists during the war through a published montage of âlots of little photosâ. He explained, however, that his editors were âa little over-fed on abstract pictures for the presentâ, which suggests why such an article did not appear.'

The Bathers, with Ship belongs to a small and exceptionally important group of paintings of bathers made by Christopher Wood in 1925, at the moment when his experience of the European avant[1]garde, his friendship with Pablo Picasso and his fascination with Serge Diaghilevâs Ballets Russes converged with the glamour and sensuality of the CÃ´te dâAzur. Modest in scale but remarkably ambitious in conception, the painting appears to stand close to the beginning of a sequence which would culminate later that year in Woodâs great six-fold Beach Scene with Bathers, Pier, Ships, etc., the largest and most complex painting of his career.
Three female bathers dominate the foreground. The central figure, standing in a rose-pink bathing costume, raises both arms around her head; to the left, a seated woman in a dark costume repeats almost the same gesture. At right, a third woman turns towards the spectator beneath a broad brimmed hat. Two of the women are partly undressed, introducing an unmistakable note of sensuality into the otherwise conspicuously modern imagery of seaside leisure. Beyond them a sailing vessel crosses the intensely coloured water, while a succession of pale buildings rises against the immense dark form of a mountain. Wood reduces figures, architecture and landscape alike to broad, lucid shapes, creating a composition of striking directness in which the fashionable world of the Riviera acquires an unexpectedly timeless grandeur.
The background of The Bathers, with Ship can now be identified with considerable confidence as Monte Carlo harbour, seen from the direction of Monaco-Ville and Fort Antoine. Period views from this position show the same conjunction of harbour, tiered pale architecture and the enormous mountain rising immediately behind the town. Particularly distinctive is the small cupola with its elongated finial towards the right of Woodâs architectural group, which can plausibly be identified with the HÃ´tel Beau-Rivage on the MontÃ©e de la Costa. The steep ascent, broad shoulder and descending profile of the mountain behind correspond equally closely with the historic topography. Wood has not transcribed the view mechanically. Balconies, windows, roads, villas and architectural ornament disappear, and Monte Carlo is distilled instead into a sequence of luminous geometric planes set against the massive dark form of the mountain. Yet enough is retained to preserve the identity of the place. This selective simplification is characteristic of Wood at his most sophisticated: apparent naÃ¯vetÃ© conceals a highly deliberate process of reduction.
The modest dimensions of The Bathers, with Ship, together with the specificity of its setting, raise the intriguing possibility that the painting was made during the Monte Carlo visit itself. Alternatively, it may have been painted shortly afterwards, when Wood and Gandarillas had returned to Paris and the experience of the Riviera remained fresh. His letters prove that he was painting there in watercolour; the present oil, with its unusually precise sense of place, seems in either case to stand particularly close to the immediate experience of the April journey.
This gives the painting a particular importance within Woodâs development during 1925. Here the imagined Mediterranean world of Picasso and of Le Train Bleu, the Ballets Russes production inspired by fashionable life on the CÃ´te dâAzur, is fused with an actual place Wood had just experienced. The statuesque bodies and fashionable bathing costumes belong to this modern mythology; the harbour, hotels and mountain belong to Monte Carlo itself. In this painting, theatre and experience have become almost indistinguishable.
This catalogue note is by Robert Upstone, author of the forthcoming catalogue raisonnÃ© of Christopher Wood.

Conceived and cast in 1971, Small Mincarlo is an outstanding iteration of Barbara Hepworthâs mature sculptural language. Composed of three folded brass discs held in tension by string. Titled after a small uninhabited island in the Isles of Scilly, an archipelago off the southwestern Cornish coast, Small Mincarlo is a meditation on the poetic possibilities of sculptural line, material and form. Belonging to the final edition that Hepworth produced with string, a material she began working with in 1939, the present work is a landmark not only of Hepworthâs oeuvre but of the history of Modern art.
Small Mincarlo illustrates Hepworthâs enduring fascination with negative space: the spiralled, golden strings delicately tracing and defining the void within the sphere suggested by the golden discs. The pierced apertures of each facet create an endless multiplicity of sightlines which, amplified by the reflectivity of the gold and spiralled string, evoke the artistâs lifelong exploration into formal presence and absence.
The rhythmic arrangement of string, the repetition of the circular form and the luminous qualities of the gold evoke a sense of cosmic harmony, inspired by the land, sea and sky of the Scillian coast. Intimate in scale, Small Mincarlo is a deeply personal iteration of the artistâs lifelong interrogation into the possibilities of sculptural form. As Hepworth noted: âI, the sculptor, am the landscape. I am the form and I am the hollow, the thrust and the contourâ (Barbara Hepworth, quoted in Sophie Bowness (ed.), op. cit., p. 144). 
Small Mincarlo represents the culmination of Hepworthâs unwavering exploration into sculptural materials, evincing her appreciation of the heightened sense of preciousness and luminosity that gold affords. At once weightless and meticulously defined Small Mincarlo embodies Hepworthâs iconic sculptural language at its most assured, poised and sophisticated.

Terry Frostâs work is characterised by brilliant colour, geometric forms and an interest in light, movement and rhythm. Through colour, Frost believed that painting could invoke deep emotion, and the present work Blue Black Arrow is an example of this embrace to its fullest extent. During the 1960s, when the present work was painted, Frost developed a distinctive visual language based on circles, arcs and stripes combined with a use of pure colour, aiming to induce a joyful sensory response from the viewer through its abstract form.
In the 1950s, Frost had spent time in St Ives, Cornwall, where the British modernists first started experimenting with a new visual language- inspired by the sea, sky and sunlight of the surrounding natural environment. In the 1960s, Frost had moved to Oxfordshire with his wife, and was teaching part time at Coventry Art College and Reading University, and these experiences fully formed the artistic expression we see in Blue Black Arrow.
This celebration of abstract art was a movement happening in both Britain and the United States. After visiting the first British exhibition of American Abstract Expressionism at the Tate Gallery in 1956, Frost first went to America in 1960 and through Clement Greenberg, one of the leading art critics of the time, met some of the Abstract Expressionist painters, including Mark Rothko, Barnett Newman and Willem de Kooning.
The contrast of the strong compositional structure with a freer, more animated application of paint may reflect Frostâs response to his time in the United States: âThe change of style seems to show Frost wishing to signal his delight in all sorts of visual stimuli â¦ It also marks a move towards a greater commitment to a decorative abstraction, completely detached from any specific literal meaningâ. (Chris Stephens, Terry Frost, St Ives Artists, Tate Publishing, London 2000, p.57.)

Conceived and cast in 1972, Conjunction XVIII belongs to his sustained exploration of relationship as a sculptural subject: how forms establish identity through proximity, balance and difference. Its title invites a reading centred on connection, while leaving the nature of that connection unresolved. Here, conjunction becomes both a formal proposition and a metaphor for the complexities of human association.
Bronze gives this sculpture a particular material authority. Its solidity anchors Chadwickâs characteristic dialogue between geometric structure and bodily suggestion, allowing abstract form to carry the implications of posture and attitude. Throughout his mature sculpture, an inclination or shift of balance can assume the expressive responsibility ordinarily assigned to facial features. His figures communicate through their physical organisation; emotion resides in the disposition of mass. The present work offers a scale suited to close, sustained looking, encouraging attention to the relationship between the sculptural object and the space surrounding it.
Chadwickâs early experience in architectural draughtsmanship and design formed his sensitivity to structure, while his experiments with mobiles established balance as a generative principle. The development towards figurative sculpture extended that principle into a psychological register. Within this trajectory, Conjunction XVIII can be understood as a mature investigation of the expressive possibilities of association, where formal equilibrium suggests questions of affinity, independence and mutual dependence.
This inquiry developed from one of the defining achievements of post-war British sculpture. Chadwickâs participation in the 1952 Venice Biennale situated him within the generation associated with Herbert Readâs âgeometry of fearâ; his International Sculpture Prize followed in 1956. By 1972, that historical language provided a foundation for an increasingly sustained examination of human presence and relationship.
Conjunction XVIII gives this continuing investigation a concentrated bronze form. Its significance lies in Chadwickâs capacity to make structure expressive without fixing its meaning. The workâs enduring proposition is that a relationship can be articulated through sculpture while remaining open to interpretation: connection given substance, yet retaining the ambiguity of lived experience.

âMy pictures are painted to be "listened" toâ¦ I should like things to fall into place with so clear a notion that the spectatorâs eye and "aesthetic ear" shall receive a clear message, a clear tune. I seek to recreate the truth of nature by making my own song about it (in paint)â¦ this creation must satisfy me as being true to life, though not naturalistically accurateâthe Artist, âNotes on Paintingâ, reproduced in Peter Khoroche, Ivon Hitchens, Lund Humphries, Aldershot, 2007, p.81 Figure, Courtyard â Greenleaves belongs to a moment when Hitchens was discovering his rhythm as a painter, developing a language in which landscape painting and abstraction are held together in an effortless embrace. Here, the figurative subject extends that enquiry, making the relationship between a person and their surroundings the foundation of a pictorial composition.
In the present work, the courtyard provides a framework of enclosure, while the figure introduces a human scale. Such a setting offered Hitchens the possibility of treating space simultaneously as a recognisable environment and as an arrangement of forms upon the canvas. The subject and the paintingâs independent rhythms remain in productive dialogue.
Hitchensâs sensitivity to its weight, density and movement was central to his achievement, and helps explain his importance to a younger generation of abstract painters, including Patrick Heron, Roger Hilton and Peter Lanyon. Across his work, broad sweeps and abbreviated marks, passages of substantial pigment and lighter applications, became instruments for translating perception into pictorial rhythm. This vocabulary allowed colour and brushwork to convey the experience of a subject while retaining their own material vitality.The present painting belongs to the formative years of that language. Hitchensâs engagement with French modernism, particularly CÃ©zanne and Matisse, encouraged him to explore how colour and structure could articulate space without depending upon conventional illusionism. His distinctive response remained rooted in familiar subjects, whose visual possibilities he continually reconsidered.
Figure, Courtyard â Greenleaves consequently enriches an understanding of Hitchens beyond landscape alone. Its combination of figure and setting demonstrates the breadth of an enquiry that would shape his subsequent career. Within the intimate compass of a courtyard, he found material for a larger artistic proposition: that observed life could be transformed into painting whose rhythm, structure and physical presence sustain an experience of their own.

The Tate Gallery has a similar painting from 1943 in its collection, titled Flowers (N06133). These flower paintings from the early 1940s occupy an interesting place in his oeuvre: Bomberg was unfortunately rejected by the War Artist's Advisory Committee. In 1942 he was commissioned to make a painting of a bombstore, but the resulting work was considered to be too imaginative. Between 1939 and 1944, he applied (unsuccessfully) for over three hundred teaching posts, in the hope of finding a position more sympathetic to his own artistic ideals. Despondent, his wife Lilian hoped to cheer him up by bringing home flowers. He then painted a number of works of this subject in 1943, and continued to buy flowers from the early morning market at Covent Garden.
The flower pictures of this time share the explosive energy of the bombstore subjects and indicate Bomberg's renewed vigour and enjoyment of painting. The present lot features pink and purple blooms and a flurry of marks which compose the background, suggesting the artist's energetic approach to and enjoyment of painting this subject.

Throughout his long career, Leon Kossoff remained deeply engaged with the world immediately around him, finding enduring inspiration in the everyday landscapes of London. Repeatedly depicting the streets, railway lines, churches, flower stalls and bustling stations near his home, he brought to these familiar subjects a profound sense of personal connection. His works reveal an intimate understanding of the city, capturing the rhythms and nuances of life within a constantly changing metropolis. Though he often revisited the same locations, shifts in light, weather, season and atmosphere ensured that each drawing and painting emerged as a distinct encounter rather than a repetition. As he noted:
âLondon, like the paint I use, seems to be in my blood stream. It's always moving â the skies, the streets, the buildings, the people who walk past me when I draw have become part of my lifeâ (Leon Kossoff, quoted in Leon Kossoff (exh. cat.), Tate, London, 1996, p.36).
The present work also bears a visual resemblance to the work of Francis Bacon, with the sense of movement that he captures so distinctly in almost ghostly figures.

This is the most striking and richly coloured self portrait by David Bowie ever to appear on the auction market. Completed in 1996, in the present lot he gazes out directly at the viewer, prominently displaying his famously asymmetric eyes, with one pupil much larger than the other, giving the impression of two different coloured irises. Even more personally, the work also features two handprints by the artist placed on either side in the lower corners of the work. 
David Bowie drew on a rich number of artistic influences as a collector, artist and musician. One of his most creative and celebrated periods were his Berlin years (1976-1979), when he was immersed in the culture and produced a fantastic trio of albums: Low, Heroes and Lodger. In addition, he also collected German Expressionist Prints, and the Germanic influence comes across particularly strongly in this work. He was also inspired by and collected works by the School of London artists Leon Kossoff and Frank Auerbach, and the portrait subject - which fills the page - and expressive handling of the medium harks back to both of these artists. Sotheby's record-breaking sale of David Bowie's art collection, Bowie/Collector, held in these rooms in 2016, celebrated his incredible collection of predominantly Modern British Art and Memphis Design.

description_block:
The present lot is offered together with a copy of the 2001 Sean Scully: Light to Dark exhibition catalogue at Galerie Lelong, Paris, in which it is included.

"You can do certain things with painting... you cannot do with anything else. With a painting, you can contain within borders a lot of experience, narrative, emotion, poetry, idea, thought, time, references and so on... Painting has a unique potential to stop time and compact feelings and experience."Sean Scully quoted in: Sean Scully: Body of Light, National Gallery of Australia In Passenger Line Orange, Sean Scully transforms the fundamental elements of painting, line, colour, and surface, into a composition of remarkable visual immediacy. Executed in 2001, the work is organised around a succession of horizontal bands whose restrained geometry is animated by subtle variations of colour and touch. The neutral colours of the work lend the composition a particular warmth and intensity, while the inset panel introduces a moment of interruption, drawing the eye into a separate but intimately connected pictorial space. The resulting image is both ordered and unsettled, its apparent simplicity giving way to a more complex experience of movement and pause.
The horizontal line has occupied a central position within Scullyâs practice since the 1980s, when the artist began to move decisively away from his earlier figurative work. Yet his paintings are never purely exercises of geometric abstraction. The individual bands retain evidence of their making, allowing the physical process of painting to remain present beneath the apparent regularity of the composition. Edges shift, colours meet imperfectly and the painted surface acquires a sense of weight and density. Rather than suppressing these irregularities in pursuit of an idealised geometry, Scully allows them to become an essential part of the workâs visual language.
This tension is heightened by the inset panel. Set within the larger structure like a crevice, it establishes a second register of colour and space, disrupting the continuity of the horizontal bands. The device creates a sense of depth without relying upon conventional illusionism: the painting seems simultaneously to advance and recede, drawing the viewer between its different planes.
Colour is equally important to this spatial experience. The orange does not simply occupy the surface but appears to generate an atmosphere around which the darker bands are organised. Its warmth gives the work a distinctly human presence, countering the potentially impersonal character of its geometric framework.
Ultimately, Passenger Line Orange demonstrates Scullyâs ability to invent abstraction with physical and emotional resonance. Through the measured repetition of its bands and the disruptive presence of the inset, the work proposes abstraction not as a fixed system, but as a continually shifting encounter between structure, colour and the human hand.

The crucifixion scene is one of Craigie Aitchisonâs most recognisable subjects, where Christ is depicted amongst an empty, surreal background in non-naturalistic colours. Throughout his career, Aitchison continued to return to the Crucifixion scene- each time altering the colours, scale, landscape, position of the cross and surrounding figures, such as the inclusion of animals. The present work is a fine example of a piece from this important body of work, being on a large scale and using deep, striking colours.
Aitchison approaches the famed subject in a non-conventional manner, instead transforming the religious motif into a modern take on human suffering, solitude, and compassion. From an early age, Aitchison was strongly influenced by Italian medieval and early Renaissance painting, particularly artists such as Giotto, whose simplified figures and emotionally expressive figures can be seen to Craigieâs modern style. Here, Christ and the surrounding landscape are depicted in a purposely simplified method: reduced down to a sequence of flat, pure colour planes. It is a reflective and spiritual image of the iconic scene, rather than one of violence, resulting in a purposely aesthetic and unique take on a timeless subject.

description_block:
Bernard Meadows studied at the Norwich School of Art from 1934-6, and later became Henry Mooreâs first assistant. Moore went on to become a close friend and mentor and indeed Meadows took great inspiration from the older artist's work initially, with his early work resembling that of Mooreâs, with undulating forms and perfectly smooth surfaces. By the 1960s, however, Meadows had departed artistically from his mentor, having found a distinct style of his own. This can be clearly seen in the present lot, Large Standing Armed Figure.
Bernard Meadows was one of the artists whose work was described by Herbert Read as capturing the 'Geometry of Fear', a term he coined in 1952 when reviewing the British pavilion at the Venice Biennale where Meadows was exhibiting work alongside that of his contemporaries including Kenneth Armitage, Lynn Chadwick and Reg Butler. Moreover, geopolitical tensions were to rise further against the backdrop of the Second World War as the 1950s and 60s progressed, and this work reflects intimately the increasing hostility that beset the world's stage at this time. 1962 formed the very peak of the Cold War, with the Cuban Missile Crisis taking the United States and Soviet Union closer to nuclear war than at any other time in history.
Created the very same year, in Large Standing Armed Figure Meadows sculpts a rough, visceral form that stands resolute against attack. One may also draw parallels to his earlier motif of the crab - including his Black Crab of 1952 - and he described these creatures as âvehicles expressing [his] feelings about humansâ. Here he seems to make a human almost crab-like, it's hard shell transmuted into the hunched monolithic back of the armed figure. His contemporary in the Geometry of Fear group, Lynn Chadwick, also began to deconstruct human forms into coarse block-like shapes, making them into more simplified archetypes, with featureless faces. 
This life-size bronze is imposing and powerful, the figureâs heavy body almost precarious upon two spindly legs. A spear-like form juts out from either side of its torso. This antagonistic, sharp bronze is characteristic of Meadowâs work at the time, reflecting a collective unease that can be seen across the sculptures produced by him and his peers.
Meadows was a master of contrast in his sculptures, and here the jutting forms of the figure's arms which appear to be encased in armature is contrasted with a harsher texturing of the surface, and the sharp points of the spears. This contrast extends to the subject too; one gets a sense of the protective nature of the figure, hunched in on itself and with crossed arms, not directly attacking but perhaps in a self-comforting gesture. Its legs are skeletal and rooted into the base, as if frozen to the spot. Capturing the essence of its time, the sculpture is universal in its relevance, as impactful today as when it was created.

He finally escaped in the spring of 1946 and, for the rest of his long life, his art became an explosion of brilliant line, light and colour drawing on ancient and modern Aegean themes. He was one of those fortunate people who get what they want and are not disappointed, but his personal odyssey was at times rocky and stormy.
In January 1967 a Craxton retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery was not well received. The artist thought he was done with Britain forever, but that Easter his adopted world fell apart when a clique of colonels staged a coup in Athens and Greece came under martial law. An anarchic spirit who had mocked authority once too often was summarily ejected from his harbourside house and studio in a crumbling Venetian palazzo on Crete. As a friend put it: 'Johnny had to leave Greece when his jokes ran away with him.'
An astonished and desolated exile wandered around and beyond the Mediterranean. From North Africa to southern Italy he often found himself wretched among ancient Greek ruins. In nine years of expulsion, when fearful that separation might last forever, he eventually settled grumpily in Edinburgh ('They call it the Athens of the North. I call it the Inverness of the South.') He drove Dovecot Weavers to distraction as they worked on his masterly and monumental Landscape with the Elements tapestry - a tribute to all things Greek - for the University of Stirling.
In 1971, while lingering in London, Craxton pined in the British Museum, musing specifically on the Parthenon marbles. The great temple to Athena on the Acropolis hill was the centrepiece of fifth century BC Athenian reconstruction overseen by the statesman Pericles after Greco-Persian Wars wreckage. Much of the surviving sculptural adornment was (in)famously removed by Lord Elgin during the Napoleonic Wars. John Craxton now felt common cause with such displacement.
He produced a series of sketches in situ, then small oil studies and this large-scale near-monochrome painting which is all the more ghostly and poignant and potent given the artist's normally joyful preoccupation with bright colour. It is a testament to loss, but also to resilience. The assembly still pulsates with the arteries and sinews of life.Craxton was no recorder of conflict - almost all his pictures are love affairs - and so the mythic Parthenon battles involving gods, giants and centaurs are not a spur for him, however much he admired them. He is inspired here by the temple's interior frieze depicting the annual Panathenaic procession in homage to Athena. Young men mount horses and a cavalcade picks up speed and purpose as the scene unfolds. The impact is impressive and uplifting - galvanising the philhellenic artist in his dream of a homeward journey.
 In Greece John Craxton was the unparalleled portraitist of people, cats and goats in a landscape stretching from mythological to modern times. This unique human and equine panorama reveals a love and yearning for Greece at its most essential. Ian Collins
Writer and curator Ian Collins is the author of John Craxton: A Life of Gifts, Yale University Press.

description_block:
In January and February 1914 Duncan Grant paid an extended visit to Tunisia. After a time spent in the capital, he went to the city of Tozeur in the south-west of the country, bordering the Sahara. He found a village pottery on the outskirts and worked there, sending back native pots for sale at the Omega Workshops, as well as at least two vases he had decorated with figures in black outline (both are now in Grantâs studio at Charleston).
The present painting shows a grove of palm trees, one of many in the district in Tozeur known as the Palmeraie. Its dates were famous and formed a chief export business of the city. Grant also sent to London a box of oranges and lemons for Vanessa Bell which she and Roger Fry both painted.
Dating from 1914, the present work demonstrates the pivotal moment that Grant decided to break from traditional English painting and embrace the European avant-garde. His time spent in North Africa and the South of France were crucial in following the steps of artists such as Matisse and Derain, the former he met in 1911 at his studio at Issy-Les-Moulineaux on the outskirts of Paris. Grant visited Matisse several times prior to his Tunisian visits. The trip ro Tunis had also inspired Grant to paint designs on local ceramics, which would later inspire the Omega Workshop, run by the Bloomsbury artists.
Grant had been exposed to the Post-Impressionists and Fauvists through Roger Fry's exhibition in London in 1910 and 1912, which had been initially met with great controversy. Grant, as a trailblazing artist of his time, was one of the few British artists to embrace the European sensibility. The Landscape in Tunis celebrates this rare period of work which left a great impression on Grant, and in the present work, he employs stylised sun-soaked colour palm leaves and gestural pencil lines, which create a wonderful sense of Mediterranean rhythm.
The importance of this work is shown by the fact that it was kept and treasured within the family collection for many years. This special group of Bloomsbury works was formerly in the collection of Frances âFannyâ Garnett, who is the daughter of Angelica Bell and David Garnett, and granddaughter to Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant. The group encompasses paintings by both Grant and Bell, who were the central figures of the Bloomsbury group working in the early twentieth century. As the second generation of Bloomsbury, Fanny grew up surrounded by painting, writing and artistic experimentation, and these personal works include familiar, family scenes to the Garnett family, including a portrait of Vanessa Bell with Julian Bell (Angelicaâs half brother) and a portrait of Nerissa Garnett (Frannyâs twin).
 We would like to thank Richard Shone for his contribution to this catalogue note.

description_block:
Painted circa 1940, The Blue Tablecloth by Anne Redpath was created several years after her return to Scotland in 1934, after she had spent fourteen years in France with her young family. Her husband, Jim Michie, settled in London in search of work while she returned to Hawick with their sons and moved back into the family home at Orchard Terrace with her parents and sister Nancy. With her three sons at school, Redpath was finally free to paint without interruption and this heralded a new burst of sustained activity, further motivated by the necessity of earning her living as a painter, as funds did not always appear regularly to support the family from her husband in London.  
The still lifes and landscapes around Hawick now formed her subject matter, and she took up her brushes with a renewed vigour, but commented that:âtaking up art again is different from music. The actual technique doesnât matter quite so much as it would in music. But at first it is difficult to attain the same kind of abandon and bravura in your painting.â (Anne Redpath, quoted in Patrick Bourne, Anne Redpath 1895 â 1965, Atelier Books Ltd, Edinburgh, 3rd edition, 2004, p.31.)
However she did indeed recapture the vim and energy with which she had painted as student, where enrolled at Edinburgh College of Art, where she had received many accolades and flourished, going on be awarded a travelling scholarship worth Â£150 in 1919, marking her out as the most promising student of her year. Settled now in Hawick, and determined to make her mark, she was elected a Professional Member of the Society of Scottish Artists in 1934. She came to favour working in the studio above all, and such still lifes as the present work became particular favourites, for the variety of compositions and interactions between objects that she could create. In 1939, she inherited a sum of money on the death of her father and this enabled her to buy a house of her own in Beaconsfield Terrace, Hawick. What resulted from this new environment was an increasing intimacy in her compositional arrangements, a delight in the placing of domestic objects and a tightness of execution that gives a vibrancy to each painting.
The Blue Tablecloth displays a mastery of form and colour that illustrates Redpathâs delight in this exploration. Clustered atop a blue tablecloth in an apparently casual arrangement sits a jug of white flowers, their full blooms encircling sunshine-yellow centres, the table top displaying in perfect contrapuntal balance all the accoutrements of domestic life: an array of cups and saucers, a teapot, a book and some apples. The light hits the scene, making the teacups shine a dazzling white, suggesting the near-translucence of porcelain in bright sunlight. The beauty of the painting is in its harmony, the careful tonal modulations of peach, blue and white, the perfectly circular apples and curving arcs of each piece of tablewear, the cosy domesticity which is conjured with artful ease. Redpathâs particular flair can be seen in all its exquisite beauty, making us look again at an apparently ordinary domestic scene with new eyes: all at once light, familiar and refreshing, a delight for the senses.

description_block:
Picking a Quarrel, executed in 1968/9, is an iconic example of Edward Burraâs assured, more mature output. 
Following the war, Burraâs travels became more limited, largely as a result of his ill health, and he instead explored Britain and Ireland, particularly the rugged landscapes of Cornwall and the Lake District. He became increasingly drawn to scenes of natural beauty and its destruction and moved away from his focus of painting people. In the aftermath of the postwar industrial revolution, Burra lamented the damage inflicted on the countryside, as seen in the present work, where monstrous diggers excavate a mountain, and in Cornish Clay Mines, painted just one year later, depicting mine shafts and a petrol station.
Here, shadowy men scale the cliff, while vibrant trucks trundle alongside them, obscured by what appear to be drips of red. Above them, a saintly figure hovers, presiding over the scene with a sense of power â or is it one of helplessness? From the figureâs halo streams red, and either way, the work is resplendent with irony.
Whilst some passages evoke the style of Burraâs earlier output, such as the iconic flattened perspective and watercolour â like painterly areas on the right, the colour here seems remarkably vibrant â in stark contrast to the imagery of desolation within the present work.
Burraâs later paintings of war and environmental destruction seem particularly resonant now, both so deeply intricate and so devastating. Picking a Quarrel has been widely exhibited, including at Pallant House and, more recently, in the highly acclaimed Burra exhibition at Tate, underscoring its significance within Burraâs oeuvre and its importance as a brilliant example from this period.

description_block:
Poppies Under is a vibrant testament to Ivon Hitchensâ enduring dedication to the still life genre. He created a singular and distinctive style which is a seamless blend of abstraction and figuration, and the present work demonstrates this wonderfully in a joyful flourish of colour and form.
After exhibiting with the London Group and leading the formation of the Seven & Five Society in 1919 - a loosely constructed exhibiting body of artists including Henry Moore, Barbara Hepworth, John Piper, and later, Ben Nicholson â Hitchensâ work became increasingly unanchored from figurative representation. The groupâs freedom from current artistic convention positioned them as the avant-garde force within British art, a role further reinforced by their engagement with developments in continental Europe. Throughout the 1920s and 30s, Hitchens and his contemporaries regarded Paul CÃ©zanne as a modern master who revitalised still life and landscape genres, paving the way for the later innovations of Matisse and the Cubism of Picasso and Braque.
Like CÃ©zanne, Hitchens sought new ways to represent form, conveying its underlying structure and visceral essence in a wholly unique manner. As Patrick Heron was to note:âHis spatial grammar â the fact that he conceives of forms in space in terms of a system of flat screens of colour lying one behind another â this is purely Cubist in origin.â(Patrick Heron, âPerspectivesâ Pallant House Gallery, https://pallant.org.uk/ivon-hitchens-artistic-influences/, accessed 12 June 2025)
Although taking inspiration from continental Europe, Hitchens was also inspired by rural Britain. He created a visual language that was deeply rooted in the woodlands of Sussex and also inspired by the farmlands of Banks Head, Cumbria, where he spent the summers with Ben and Winifred Nicholson and their artist friends. It was in Banks Head that Hitchens began depicting still lifes in a manner not dissimilar to those of his panoramic landscapes. Instead of treating the still-life as a static or self-contained genre, Hitchens saw it as a stage on which experimentation and new modes of representation could be trialled. The unusual, elongated format of the canvas, allows a free flowing compositional arrangement, encouraging the viewerâs eye to experience more immersively the painterly application and assured swathes of colour.
Hitchens wrote beautifully about his own painting practice, and his work took on a lyrical resonance as his understanding of colour entwined with what he described as âthe musical appearance of thingsâ (Ivon Hitchens, Space Through Colour, Pallant House Gallery, 2019, p. 63) At this time, Hitchens regarded the elements of composition â line, form, shape, and colour â as âthe instruments of a painterâs orchestraâ (ibid., p. 63). In Poppies Under, we see a beautiful culmination of his fluid and expressive approach to painting.
